q344: For twenty years Pastor Samuel had never taken a real holiday. He preached three times on Sunday, visited the sick every afternoon, answered calls at midnight and led every wedding and funeral. His phone never left his hand. Lately he felt numb during worship and could not remember the last time he had read the Bible for himself rather than for a sermon. He had chest pains and high blood pressure. He snapped at his wife and felt nothing when church members thanked him. One Sunday he stood at the pulpit, opened his mouth and nothing came out for several seconds. He covered it up, but at home he sat in the dark and wondered if God had left him.
q345: Burnout is a state of physical, emotional and spiritual exhaustion from long stress without enough recovery. It shows up as exhaustion, emotional numbness and a sense that nothing we do matters. Samuel's stress system had been running for years without breaks, and his body was paying the price. Research suggests that long stress can affect sleep, blood pressure, mood and memory. Underneath was a belief common among ministers: if I rest, people will be let down and God will be disappointed. He had also become the only helper in the church, so everyone depended on him. His sense of worth had quietly shifted from being God's son to being God's busy servant.
q346: His doctor warned him about his heart. That same week his eldest daughter said, Appa, you pray for everyone except us. Samuel finally told the church elders the truth. To his surprise, they were relieved and offered him a month of rest.
q347: Took a month of sabbatical with his phone given to an elder
q348: Practised sitting still before God for ten minutes each morning with no agenda
q349: Lay down for a deep rest after lunch three times a week
q350: Started a weekly Sabbath day, protected on the church calendar
q351: Trained a team of four lay leaders to share pastoral visits
q352: Used a weekly review to notice early signs of overload
q353: Moses was wearing himself out judging the people from morning to evening, and his father-in-law said, the thing that thou doest is not good. Thou art not able to perform it thyself alone (Exodus 18:17-18). He shared the work, and the people were better served. Jesus told His tired disciples, come ye yourselves apart into a desert place, and rest a while (Mark 6:31). God commanded the Sabbath not as a burden but as a gift (Mark 2:27). The church belongs to Christ, not to the pastor. Samuel rediscovered that he is first a beloved child who abides in the vine, and only then a worker who bears fruit (John 15:5).
q354: God designed the body to work in rhythms of effort and rest. The heart, the brain and the hormones all need recovery. Research suggests that regular rest, sleep and time away from work help bring stress hormones back to healthy levels and protect the heart. In studies, quiet, unhurried rest allows the brain to process, restore attention and reconnect with meaning. Sharing the load also lowers stress, because we were made to carry burdens together, not alone. The weekly Sabbath is God's built-in reset for a body that was never meant to run nonstop.
q355: Mark 6:31|And he said unto them, Come ye yourselves apart into a desert place, and rest a while.
q359: After the sabbatical, Samuel's blood pressure came down with medicine and rest. The numbness lifted slowly over several months. Some weeks he slipped back into long days, especially during festivals and funerals, and he still struggles with guilt when he rests. But his preaching has a fresh warmth, his family sees more of him, and the church has grown healthier with shared leadership.
q360: A minister's first calling is to be with Jesus, and rest is obedience, not laziness.
q361: Even pastors get tired. God made rest days so we can be refilled like an empty cup.
q362: Arjun and the chair at the dining table
q363: Arjun, 35, bank officer in Mumbai, married, eldest son whose father died suddenly
q364: Arjun's father died of a heart attack at sixty-two, two days before Diwali leave. Arjun arranged everything: the hospital papers, the funeral, the relatives, the food. As the eldest son he felt he had to stay strong for his mother and younger sister. He did not cry at the funeral. Back at work two weeks later, he seemed fine. But at home he could not sit at the dining table because his father's chair was there. He kept his father's last voice message on his phone and could not listen to it or delete it. Months later, a song in a shop made him run outside and weep. He felt confused, because he believed his father was with the Lord, so why did it hurt so much?
q365: Grief is the natural response of a body and mind that has loved. Research suggests that the brain holds a map of the people we love, and when someone dies, the brain takes time to update that map. This is why we expect to see them in their chair. Arjun had pushed his grief aside to cope with duties, which is common, especially for men in the role of eldest son. Grief that is held back often comes out suddenly through triggers like songs, smells or festivals. He also believed that strong Christians should not grieve deeply, which added guilt on top of sorrow.
q366: His pastor visited and simply said, Jesus wept at His friend's tomb, even knowing He would raise him. Arjun realised that grieving was not a lack of faith. That night he listened to the voice message and cried for an hour, with his wife sitting beside him.
q367: Wrote a lament to God about his father's death
q368: Wrote a letter to his father thanking him and saying what he never said
q369: Set aside one evening a week to look at photos and remember with his mother
q370: Allowed tears when grief waves came instead of running away
q371: Joined a grief group at a nearby church for eight weeks
q372: Jesus wept (John 11:35). He knew the end of the story, yet He still felt the sorrow of the moment. Paul tells us we sorrow not, even as others which have no hope (1 Thessalonians 4:13). He does not say we do not grieve. He says we grieve with hope. Many psalms are laments, honest prayers of pain, and they are part of Scripture so that grief has a voice in worship. Blessed are they that mourn, for they shall be comforted, said Jesus (Matthew 5:4). Comfort comes to those who allow themselves to mourn. Arjun's tears became prayers, and in them he met a God who understands loss.
q373: God designed us to attach deeply to those we love, so separation brings pain. Grief is the cost of love. Research suggests that grief usually comes in waves rather than straight stages, and that slowly facing the loss, with support, helps the brain adjust to the new reality. Crying can release tension and, in studies, is linked to feeling calmer afterwards. Sharing memories with others gives the loss a place in our life story. Over time the brain does not forget the person but learns to carry the love in a new way.
q374: Matthew 5:4|Blessed are they that mourn: for they shall be comforted.
q378: A year later, Arjun can sit in his father's chair at the table. The first Diwali was very hard, and he still has grief waves on his father's birthday. But he now talks about his father with smiles as well as tears. He and his mother have grown closer, and he feels more honest with God than ever before.
q379: Grieving with hope means we can cry freely while trusting that death does not have the final word.
q380: When someone we love dies, it is okay to cry. Even Jesus cried, and He helps our hearts heal slowly.
q381: Lalremruati and the quiet flat in Pune
q382: Lalremruati, 24, from Aizawl, Mizoram, newly moved to Pune for a job in a pharma company
q383: Mami, as her family called her, had grown up surrounded by people. In Aizawl there was always church, cousins and neighbours dropping in. In Pune she shared a flat with a girl who worked night shifts, and most evenings she ate instant noodles alone in her room. At work people were polite, but they spoke Marathi and Hindi among themselves and she felt like an outsider. Some people asked if she was from China, which hurt. She called home every night and cried after hanging up. On Sundays she watched her home church online instead of looking for a local one. After three months she felt hollow, and she started to wonder if moving had been a mistake.
q384: Loneliness is a signal, like hunger, telling us we need connection. Research suggests that long loneliness raises stress hormones and keeps the brain on alert for social threats. That makes lonely people more cautious and less likely to reach out, which deepens the loneliness. Mami's move had cut her off from all her usual sources of belonging at once. Experiences of being treated as different, because of her looks or culture, made her brain expect rejection. She believed that friends should come naturally, as they had at home, and did not yet realise that building friendships in a new city takes deliberate small steps.
q385: Her mother told her on a call, You are always welcoming new people at home, maybe in Pune you will be the new person who needs welcoming. Mami realised she had been waiting for a home to find her. She decided to look for one.
q386: Visited three local churches and chose one with a young adults fellowship
q387: Used a reach-out script to invite a colleague for lunch
q388: Planned one social activity each week even when tired
q389: Noticed small glimmers each day, like a kind security guard or chai with a colleague
q391: God setteth the solitary in families (Psalm 68:6). From the beginning, God said it is not good that the man should be alone (Genesis 2:18). Ruth left her homeland and found a new people and a new home, because she clung to God and to Naomi (Ruth 1:16). The early church in Acts met daily in homes, breaking bread with gladness (Acts 2:46). In Christ, Mami was no stranger but a fellow citizen with the saints and of the household of God (Ephesians 2:19). That truth gave her courage to show up at a new fellowship, trusting that God's family exists in every city.
q392: God designed humans for belonging. Research suggests that social connection is linked with better mood, stronger immunity and even longer life. Studies also suggest that friendships grow through repeated, small time together, often many hours before people feel close. This means friendship takes patience. When we reach out, even in small ways, the brain begins to update its expectation of rejection. Noticing small moments of safety and kindness, sometimes called glimmers, helps a lonely nervous system calm down and open up. We were made to be part of a body, not to live as a single limb.
q393: Psalm 68:6|God setteth the solitary in families.
q397: It took about five months before Mami had two friends she could call. Some weekends were still lonely, and Christmas away from home was very hard. But the young adults fellowship became a second family, and she now hosts a Mizo food night for others far from home. She still misses Aizawl, but Pune is starting to feel like home too.
q398: Belonging in a new place is built slowly through small brave steps, and God's family is waiting in every city.
q399: Moving to a new place can feel lonely. Saying hello and joining a church family helps us make new friends.
q400: Neha and the scroll that stole her joy
q401: Neha, 22, final year design student in Ahmedabad, lives in a hostel
q402: Neha's evenings followed a pattern. After classes she lay on her bed and scrolled. Her classmates were posting internship offers, trips to Goa, engagement photos and perfect sketches. Old school friends had new cars and foreign degrees. An hour would pass, then two. She would put the phone down feeling ugly, behind and secretly jealous, then feel guilty for not being happy for others. She started editing her own photos heavily and deleting posts that did not get enough likes. Her prayer times became shorter, and her Bible stayed on the shelf. When her best friend got the internship Neha wanted, she could not congratulate her and avoided her for a week.
q403: Social media shows us everyone's highlight reel, and our brain compares it with our own behind-the-scenes life. Humans naturally compare to know where they stand, but the brain was not designed to compare with hundreds of people at once. Each like and notification gives a small hit of dopamine, the brain's reward chemical, which keeps us scrolling even when it makes us feel worse. Research suggests that heavy, passive scrolling is linked with lower mood and envy in some people. Neha's deeper belief was that her worth depended on being successful and admired, a message she had absorbed from years of rankings and marks.
q404: During a power cut at the hostel, Neha spent an evening without her phone, talking with her roommate on the terrace. She felt lighter than she had in months. She realised the scroll was not just wasting time, it was shaping how she saw herself and God.
q405: Deleted two apps from her phone and kept one with a thirty-minute daily limit
q406: Swapped evening scrolling for a short walk or sketching for herself
q407: Wrote three gratitudes every night before sleep
q408: Noticed comparison thoughts and said, I am having the thought that I am behind
q409: Called her best friend, apologised and congratulated her
q410: Peter, after Jesus told him about his own future, looked at John and asked, Lord, and what shall this man do? Jesus answered, what is that to thee? Follow thou me (John 21:21-22). God has a unique path for each of us. Paul warns that those who measure themselves by comparing among themselves are not wise (2 Corinthians 10:12). Envy, says Proverbs, is the rottenness of the bones (Proverbs 14:30). The cure is not pretending to be happy but returning to gratitude and our own calling. Neha is God's workmanship, created for good works prepared for her (Ephesians 2:10). Her life is not a race against her classmates.
